findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Deep Dive - CR2 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Officers have progressed schemes outside agreed appraisal and governance process; directorate priorities can conflict with corporate financial priorities
findings.detail: The risk identifies that a driver is 'Officers progressing schemes outside the agreed appraisal, prioritisation and governance process, or directorate priorities conflicting with corporate financial priorities, leading to uncoordinated investment decisions and weakened corporate oversight.' This indicates prior breaches of governance discipline.
findings.matters: Schemes bypassing affordability challenge and corporate oversight can lock the council into commitments it cannot afford, and conflicting priorities suggest weak central financial control.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Officers progressing schemes outside the agreed appraisal, prioritisation and governance process, or directorate priorities conflicting with corporate financial priorities, leading to uncoordinated investment decisions and weakened corporate oversight

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Deep Dive - CR2 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Capital schemes required to deliver revenue benefits, with 'overstated business cases' identified as risk to sustainable programme
findings.detail: The council lists as a key CR2 risk driver: 'Requirement for capital schemes to deliver revenue benefit, increasing sensitivity to business case assumptions.' The risk description identifies 'overstated business cases' as one of the potential causes of failure to deliver a sustainable capital programme.
findings.matters: If capital schemes are expected to generate revenue savings or income to justify themselves, then optimistic forecasting creates a cliff: schemes underdeliver on revenue benefits, squeezing already-pressured revenue budgets.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Requirement for capital schemes to deliver revenue benefit, increasing sensitivity to business case assumptions

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Deep Dive - CR2 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Council maintains comparatively low usable reserves, limiting resilience to financial shocks while managing capital programme risk
findings.detail: The Financial Management Assurance Report, covering March 2025 to March 2026, notes 'The Council maintains a comparatively low level of usable reserves, limiting resilience to financial shocks.' This constraint is highlighted in the context of managing the CR2 capital programme risk.
findings.matters: Low reserves combined with increasing reliance on borrowing and revenue pressure from capital spending creates a fragile financial position with little buffer for programme delays or cost overruns.
findings.figures: None specified; reserve level noted as 'comparatively low'
findings.quote: The Council maintains a comparatively low level of usable reserves, limiting resilience to financial shocks

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Deep Dive - CR2 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Council uses one-off capital receipts to fund ongoing revenue expenditure, with MTFS targeting reduction 'over time'
findings.detail: The document identifies 'The use of capital receipts to support revenue expenditure' as a key risk driver. The Medium-Term Financial Strategy includes actions to 'reduce reliance on capital receipts for revenue funding over time,' indicating this is currently a material budget component but the council recognises it is not sustainable.
findings.matters: Using one-off capital receipts to plug revenue holes masks underlying budget stress and signals the council is not solving the structural problem, only deferring it.
findings.figures: None specified

findings.paper_title: Corporate Risk Register Deep Dive - CR2 Capital Programmes
findings.headline: Capital programme risk formally rated YELLOW with likelihood 3 and impact 4, driven by reliance on borrowing creating revenue budget pressure
findings.detail: The council has assessed CR2 (capital programme risk) as YELLOW with a likelihood score of 3 and impact score of 4. A key driver is 'Increasing reliance on borrowing and limited internal funding capacity, placing pressure on revenue budgets.' This is part of a wider set of drivers including weak long-term asset planning and capacity constraints in delivery.
findings.matters: A formally rated yellow risk on capital programme sustainability is a material concern for lenders assessing debt capacity and covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Likelihood 3, Impact 4, YELLOW RAG score 12
findings.quote: Increasing reliance on borrowing and limited internal funding capacity, placing pressure on revenue budgets

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: An audit management system error caused 48 recommendations to become hidden, complicating tracking of remediation progress.
findings.detail: Following a configuration change to Pentana (the audit management system), 48 recommendations became 'hidden' and could not be located through normal reporting. This was discovered only when known outstanding recommendations could not be found. The issue has been resolved, but the council is still working to ascertain the status of all affected recommendations.
findings.matters: If audit recommendations can disappear from the tracking system, the council loses visibility of control obligations and cannot reliably report on remediation. This materially weakens the audit trail and governance assurance.
findings.figures: 48 recommendations affected by the system error
findings.quote: Following a configuration change, certain recommendations became 'hidden', which was discovered when known outstanding recommendations could not be located within the system or through reporting functions. This issue has now been resolved. 48 outstanding recommendations were affected by this system error.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: Internal Audit has encountered a vacancy and sickness absence that has deferred multiple audits to 2026/27, reducing current oversight coverage.
findings.detail: The audit team has had an unexpected vacancy and periods of sickness absence that have reduced available resources. As a result, multiple planned audits have been deferred to 2026/27, including those on flexi-time, traffic enforcement, PCI, unsafe buildings, markets, and four schools. Additionally, 15 audits that are ongoing or in draft will not be finalized until 2026/27.
findings.matters: If the internal audit function is understaffed and falling behind, the council loses real-time visibility of control weaknesses. A lender needs assurance that audit findings are being identified and acted on promptly.
findings.figures: 6 audits deferred; 15 audits ongoing or in draft; resource impact reported in 2025/26 plan
findings.quote: Since the last reporting period, Internal Audit have had an unexpected vacancy, and a number of team members have had periods of sickness absence. This has impacted on the available resources, and the ability to complete audit assignments.

findings.headline: Audit recommendations are aging faster than they are being closed; Finance & Resources has a 100% increase in aged recommendations.
findings.detail: Between January and May 2026, aged audit recommendations (over 12 months old) increased from 44 to 55 outstanding. Essential/Strategic aged recommendations grew from 10 to 17. Finance & Resources directorate saw a 100% increase in aged recommendations—from 6 to 12. This signals either slow remediation or deteriorating control execution.
findings.matters: A growing backlog of old audit findings, especially in finance, suggests the council is not executing on agreed control improvements. This weakens overall governance and raises the risk that identified weaknesses persist in current operations.

findings.headline: Budget oversight and stakeholder engagement have 'Limited' assurance; key evidence is missing from Children's and Homelessness Services.
findings.detail: The audit of stakeholder engagement in budget management found weaknesses in budget governance and oversight, with key evidence not available in Children's and Homelessness Services to demonstrate clear budget-holder accountability, communication of the 2025/26 budget, or routine budget monitoring. Evidence gaps limited the audit scope and contributed to the 'Limited' assurance opinion.
findings.matters: If key service areas cannot produce evidence of budget accountability or routine monitoring, overspends may not be detected in time. Homelessness and children's services are typically high-risk budget areas.
findings.figures: 2 Essential/Strategic and 3 High recommendations issued
findings.quote: Key evidence was not available in Children's and Homelessness Services to demonstrate clear budget-holder accountability, communication of the 2025/26 budget, and routine budget monitoring through Directorate Management Teams. These evidence gaps limited the scope of audit testing and contributed to the limited assurance opinion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: Procurement card spending has no central oversight and operates on a 2016 policy that is now outdated.
findings.detail: The audit found there is no central record of who holds procurement cards, with management responsibility scattered across services with no clear corporate ownership. The Procurement Card Policy has not been reviewed since 2016. Data analytics was not even undertaken as part of the audit because fundamental control weaknesses were identified first. The audit opinion is 'Limited'.
findings.matters: Procurement cards can be a vector for unauthorized spending, fraud, or policy violation if not centrally managed and monitored. Absence of a cardholder register and analytics suggests the council cannot detect patterns of misuse.
findings.figures: 4 Essential/Strategic recommendations issued
findings.quote: There is no central record of cardholders, with responsibility for card management operating at service level and no clear overall corporate ownership. The current Procurement Card Policy and procedures have not been reviewed since 2016 and require updating to reflect additional controls identified through this audit.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report
findings.headline: Emergency temporary housing arrangements operating without formal contracts or effective controls.
findings.detail: Liverpool uses an emergency arrangement with Click Travel to provide interim and temporary accommodation for homeless families, but this arrangement has never been formalized into a contract. The audit found no reliable mechanism to confirm client check-in and check-out with suppliers, no reconciliations are being undertaken, and processes lack transparency. The audit opinion is 'Limited', indicating significant gaps in the control framework.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled spending on emergency accommodation, which is often expensive and high-volume in councils under housing pressure, exposes the council to overpayment, supplier fraud, and audit failure. A lender needs assurance that expenditure on temporary housing is tracked and verified.
findings.figures: 5 Essential/Strategic recommendations issued
findings.quote: An emergency arrangement is in place between LCC and Click Travel, originally established to support corporate travel but subsequently extended to secure Interim Accommodation and TA for homeless families and individuals. However, these arrangements are not supported by formally agreed contractual terms. The current control framework is not operating effectively: processes lack transparency, there is no reliable mechanism for confirming client check-in and check-out with suppliers, and reconciliations are not being undertaken.

findings.matters: Restructuring away from short-term borrowing reduces refinancing risk if credit markets tighten, but extends the council's fixed debt maturity profile. The £129.5m shift indicates significant maturing debt successfully refinanced.

findings.detail: PWLB borrowing rose from £702.4m to £735.6m between November and February. findings.paper_title: 06. Appendix A - Annex 4 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Homelessness programs targeting £11.8m in annual cost avoidance, the council's largest single savings dependency
findings.detail: The council is investing in homelessness transformation programs claiming £11.8m in annual cost avoidance: £6m from reducing nightly rates and housing benefit costs, £4.1m from reducing temporary accommodation, £1.4m from prevention, and £0.3m from Camden Place emergency provision. findings.headline: Council requires £22.912m in capital receipts but currently holds only £9.628m, creating a £13.284m funding dependency
findings.detail: The council's transformation and capital program across 2025/26-2030/31 requires £22.912m in capital receipts. findings.paper_title: 12a. Appendix B - Capital & Asset Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Council holds £35m LOBO loans and faces interest rate refinancing risk on maturing short-term debt
findings.detail: The council holds £35m of Lender Option Borrower Option loans and has significant short-term borrowing due for refinancing. It experienced material cost increases when interest rates rose in 2022/23 and 2023/24. The strategy notes it will "continue to defer the point at which long term debt is arranged" pending rate forecasts, creating ongoing exposure to further increases.
findings.matters: Council is vulnerable to interest rate shocks affecting debt service costs. Strategy is explicitly deferring long-term refinancing, betting on falling rates; if rates rise further, revenue budget impact will be sharp.
findings.figures: £35m LOBO loans outstanding; £30m LOBO loans repaid 2023/24 with £1.9m discount; gross debt forecast £1,116m (2026/27) rising to £1,250m (2029/30–2030/31)
findings.quote: the significant movement in interest rates during 2022/23 & 2023/24 has increased the cost of re-financing this borrowing and this has been reflected with the interest payable estimates included in the MTFS... the current strategy is to continue to defer the point at which long term debt is arranged. Given the uncertainty and current interest rate exposure it will be prudent to look for opportunities to reduce interest rate exposure in a gradual manner over the next 12 months.

findings.paper_title: 12a. Appendix B - Capital & Asset Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Construction cost inflation and global tensions explicitly creating delivery and cost risk to all capital budgets
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that construction industry cost escalation, exacerbated by global tensions and supply chain disruption, is creating material risk to capital programme delivery. It states budgets are "potentially subject to risk in both delivery and cost" and will need reforecasting during the year.
findings.matters: Capital budgets already tight against revenue constraints; inflation could force project deferral, scope cuts, or further borrowing. Council is signalling it expects variance against these estimates.
findings.figures: No specific inflation uplift given; contingency of £5m per annum (5% of spending) built in
findings.quote: Local authority capital programmes continue to face challenges because of on-going cost escalation in the construction industry; exacerbated by global tensions. On this basis all capital programme budgets, whilst based on the most up-to-date information and subject to monitoring throughout the year will potentially be subject to risk in both delivery and cost.

findings.paper_title: 12a. Appendix B - Capital & Asset Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising as share of revenue budget, with explicit warning that 10.3% threshold would force £20.6m additional annual service cuts
findings.detail: Capital financing costs (interest and Minimum Revenue Provision) are forecast to rise from 8.5% of net revenue stream in 2025/26 to 9.0% by 2028/29. The strategy includes a numerical warning: if this ratio reaches 10.3%, the council would need an additional £20.6m of annual savings in services to maintain balance.
findings.matters: Shows explicit crowding-out of revenue budget by capital debt service. The council is identifying the threshold at which capital financing becomes unaffordable and would force cuts to services.
findings.figures: Financing costs 8.5% (2025/26) → 7.8% (2026/27) → 8.7% (2027/28) → 9.0% (2028/29); at 10.3% would require £20.6m additional annual savings; total financing costs £64.1m–£82.1m across this period
findings.quote: The percentage of the council's revenue budget that is committed in the long term to capital financing costs is increasing, and this indicates that a greater proportion of the estimated future revenue budget is required to pay for capital financing costs... if the net debt costs as a proportion of net revenue stream indicator was to increase to 10.3% in 2026/27 this would increase the level of borrowing in the capital programme by an additional £258m... an additional £20.6m of annual capital finance costs would be incurred in the revenue budget. These additional capital financing costs would need to be offset by corresponding savings in services to maintain a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: 12a. Appendix B - Capital & Asset Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Capital receipts target of £3.56m is critical but uncertain; if missed, borrowing must substitute at direct cost to revenue budget
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly acknowledges that achieving targeted capital receipts from asset disposals is uncertain. If the council fails to generate £3.56m in receipts over five years, the only alternative is to increase borrowing, which directly increases annual revenue costs. Additionally, a separate £11.6m of receipts is earmarked to fund transformation costs.
findings.matters: Creates a binary risk: either disposals succeed and the plan holds, or they fail and borrowing (and therefore revenue financing costs) rises by the difference. Property market volatility directly threatens the capital programme feasibility.
findings.figures: £3.561m capital receipts target 2026/27–2030/31; £11.6m additional receipts needed for transformation; capital programme backed by Asset Management Plans still under development
findings.quote: the five-year capital programme is reliant on achieving £3.561m of capital receipts over the years 2026/27 to 2030/31 (plus a further £11.6m of receipts to fund revenue transformation costs in 2026/27 and 2027/28)... If the capital receipts target is not achieved, then projects can only proceed by substituting for borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 12a. Appendix B - Capital & Asset Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Five-year capital programme of £494m requires £310m of borrowing with no alternative funding sources available
findings.detail: Of the £494.2m total capital programme, borrowing funds £309.67m (63%). Grants total £173.7m, private contributions only £6.95m, and capital receipts expected to deliver just £3.56m. The programme is heavily dependent on external debt to proceed.
findings.matters: Creates a large and growing debt obligation with ongoing revenue consequences; limits the council's future borrowing capacity and creates vulnerability to interest rate movements.
findings.figures: Total programme £494.249m; Borrowing £309.670m; Grants £173.671m; Capital Receipts forecast £2.561m to £3.561m

findings.paper_title: 04. Appendix A - Annex 2 - Budget Efficiencies & Savings (2)
findings.headline: The council is funding transformation capital expenditure via borrowing, with annual financing costs charged back to services.
findings.detail: A footnote on the Adult Social Care section states 'Budget of £0.036m per annum will be transferred from this service to fund capital financing costs relating to borrowing.' This indicates the council is taking on debt to fund Extra Care and other capital-based transformations, and services are paying the cost of capital repayment from their savings.
findings.matters: This shows the council is not just cutting costs—it is borrowing to invest. The £0.036m charge suggests either small borrowing or very low-rate debt. A lender needs visibility of total capital spend planned (not shown here) and how much borrowing sits behind these transformation targets.
findings.figures: £0.036m per annum capital financing cost transfer

findings.paper_title: 04. Appendix A - Annex 2 - Budget Efficiencies & Savings (2)
findings.headline: Senior management restructure is planned for 2027/28 onwards, with savings rising from £0.5m to £1.0m by 2028/29.
findings.detail: Finance & Resources shows 'Corporate saving across the whole Council in senior management structure' starting at £0.5m in year 2 and doubling to £1.0m by year 3. This is marked as BAU savings (not transformation), meaning the council assumes it can implement headcount reductions without new investment.
findings.matters: A lender should track whether the council is cutting management to stabilise finances. If the cut is alongside other major transformations, it may signal stretched senior capacity to deliver change. If delays occur, the full £1m saving will not materialise in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: 04. Appendix A - Annex 2 - Budget Efficiencies & Savings (2)
findings.headline: Extra Care Housing expansion is the single largest savings item, worth £11.1m in 2026/27 growing to £34.5m by 2028/29.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is pinning its transformation savings almost entirely (£11.1m of £13.9m in year 1) on building new accommodation. The model assumes expanding Extra Care will reduce demand for residential and nursing care. The pathway grows steeply: £11.1m → £20.9m → £34.5m over three years, with other transformation items (digital TEC, reablement) shown but unfunded in the table.
findings.matters: This is the council's primary lever for controlling Adult Social Care costs, and it requires successful capital investment and market response. Delivery risk is high; if Extra Care adoption is slower than assumed, the £34.5m year 3 saving will not land.

findings.paper_title: 12b. Appendix B - Annex 1 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Capital expenditure programme heavily weighted to 2026/27; falls to £15.3m by 2030/31 with no grant funding.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is front-loaded at £234.6m in 2026/27 but declines sharply to £135.5m (2027/28), £58.6m (2028/29), and £54.3m (2029/30). findings.headline: Outstanding debt of £925m growing; total CFR projected to rise from £1,106.6m to £1,263.6m over three years.
findings.detail: At 31 December 2025, Liverpool's total borrowing was £925m with net debt of £854m. The Capital Financing Requirement (underlying need to borrow for capital purposes) is forecast to grow by £157m (14%) over 2025/26 to 2028/29. Anticipated external debt portfolio is projected to grow from £937m to £1,167m. This represents substantial and continuing growth in absolute debt levels.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing declines 78% from £90.1m (2025/26) to £20.1m (2028/29); external borrowing as percentage of Capital Financing Requirement rises from 91.2% to 98.3%
findings.detail: Internal borrowing (using reserves to avoid external borrowing) falls from £90.1m in 2025/26 to £20.1m by 2028/29—a 78% decline. Correspondingly, debt as a percentage of the Capital Financing Requirement rises from 91.2% to 98.3%. This represents a shift from self-funding towards dependence on external markets and exposes the council to interest rate and refinancing risk.

findings.headline: Debt of £925m; debt servicing is 7% of net revenue budget (£34.085m in 2026/27); increasing reliance on external borrowing ahead
findings.detail: Liverpool has £925m of borrowing as at 31 December 2025, costing 7% of net revenue budget to service. The CFO projects that 'plans for capital investment are reliant on increased borrowing and as internal balances decrease a greater proportion of this will be from external borrowing.' This will further increase the proportion of budgets needed for debt principal repayment (minimum revenue provision) and interest.
findings.matters: A lender measures debt-servicing burden and headroom. 7% of revenue to debt service is material. The trajectory — decreasing reserves, increasing debt reliance — shows the council is drawing down options. This matters for credit and refinancing risk.

findings.headline: Capital programme reliance on receipts creates borrowing risk; receipts shortfall forces additional borrowing or programme cuts
findings.detail: The capital programme funding is built on assumptions about capital receipt availability. The CFO flags 'risk that if receipts cannot be generated then additional borrowing costs could be incurred if the programme spend cannot be reduced.' This is acute because capital receipts are also needed for 2026/27 and 2027/28 transformation costs, competing for the same finite source.
findings.matters: Capital programmes are usually front-loaded but affordable. If receipts don't materialise, the council either abandons schemes (reputational/service risk) or borrows more (debt risk). A lender needs to know whether the receipt forecasts are realistic.
findings.figures: Capital receipts rely on 'strategic programme of asset sales'; competing use of receipts for transformation costs in 2026/27 and 2027/28

findings.paper_title: 03. Appendix A - Annex 1 - Statement on Robustness of Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves v2
findings.headline: DSG deficit funding cliff: government covers 90% of historic deficit in 2026/27 only; council will 'struggle to fund' 2026/27–28 if funding stops
findings.detail: The statutory override allowing the council to hold a negative DSG reserve ends 31 March 2028. Government has funded 90% of historic deficits through a 2026/27 grant, but the CFO explicitly warns that if additional DfE funding is not made available going forward, the council 'will struggle to fund for 2026/27 and 2027/28' — meaning the deficit will have to come from other reserves or cuts to service.
findings.matters: A cliff-edge risk: the council is relying on government discretion (not law) to survive 2027/28. If SEND demand continues and funding is not forthcoming, the council faces a structural funding gap in core education.

findings.headline: £13.445m of budgeted savings have not been delivered in 2025/26, and 'lack of permanent delivery' spans past years

A refreshed savings programme exists for 2026/27 onward, but the CFO cautions it 'will require strong governance, effective monitoring and regular and honest conversations' — acknowledging that directorates' assurances alone are not sufficient.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to deliver savings is a red flag that the council's budget is built on shaky assumptions. It suggests either poor planning, optimism bias, or capacity problems. A lender needs assurance this is being fixed.

The auditor escalated this from an improvement recommendation to a key recommendation.
findings.matters: Internal control failures create unpriced risk for a lender. If the council cannot execute its own improvement plans or embed audit recommendations, it is unlikely to hit its stated savings or revenue targets.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion issued; significant recommendations overdue 6+ months
findings.quote: Internal audit provided a Limited Assurance Internal Audit Opinion for 2024/25, indicating that there are significant control weaknesses that present a high risk to the control environment.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Homelessness Service ballooned from £13.1m overspend (2024-25) to £15.9m forecast overspend (2025-26)
findings.detail: The Homelessness Service overspent by £13.1m in 2024-25 and is now forecast to overspend by £15.9m in 2025-26—a 22% increase in just one year. The auditor notes 'Demand within the Homelessness Service also continues to create significant financial pressure and risk'. This also reflects an open 2023-24 key recommendation on cost management.
findings.matters: Homelessness is an open-ended statutory duty. Escalating overspends in this area show the council is losing control of a major cost driver, which could force disproportionate cuts elsewhere or further reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Homelessness overspend: £13.1m (2024-25); forecast £15.9m (2025-26)
findings.quote: The service overspent by £13.1m in 2024/25 and pressures continue into 2025/26 with a forecast overspend of £15.9m as at Month Five.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Children's and Adult Social Care overspends persistent: £15.5m and £3.3m in 2024-25, both forecast to overspend again in 2025-26
findings.detail: Children's Social Care overspent by £15.5m and Adult Social Care by £3.3m in 2024-25. The auditor notes both services 'have significant forecast overspends as at Month Five 2025/26'. This mirrors a key recommendation from 2023-24 that remains 'open'—the council has failed to bring these pressures under control.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether cost growth is temporary or structural. Two years of consecutive overspends in high-cost services, with no improvement forecast, suggest demand or efficiency issues the council cannot manage within budget.
findings.figures: Children's Social Care: £15.5m overspend 2024-25; Adult Social Care: £3.3m overspend 2024-25
findings.quote: Children's Social Care overspent by £15.5m in 2024/25 and Adult Social Care by £3.3m. While the Council is taking action to try to mitigate budget pressures, these services both have significant forecast overspends as at Month Five 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Savings pipeline slippage: £13.9m (19%) of £68m target undelivered as at March 2025
findings.detail: The council proposed an £85.6m three-year savings pipeline in 2023-24. By end of 2024-25, £13.9m had not been delivered—a 19% miss. For 2025-26, this £13.9m slippage is now rolled into a £41.7m savings target, and Q1 monitoring shows £13.9m of that at risk (red/amber RAG rated).
findings.matters: Savings plans that slip year-on-year signal weak programme management and eroding confidence in the council's ability to rebalance. A lender sees this as proof that stated deficit-closing plans are overstated.
findings.figures: £13.9m undelivered from £68m 2023-24/2024-25 target; £41.7m 2025-26 target; £13.9m at risk
findings.quote: there have been challenges to savings delivery, with £13.9m undelivered (19%) as at March 2025 when measured against the £68.0m total target for 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Cumulative budget deficits forecast at £26.7m (2026-27) rising to £60.3m (2027-28)
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy now forecasts a £26.7m gap in 2026-27, growing to £60.3m by 2027-28. The council acknowledges these gaps 'must' be bridged by a Transformation Programme that is 'essential' to financial sustainability, but delivery to date has been patchy.
findings.matters: A lender is pricing medium-term creditworthiness. A £60m structural deficit in 18 months, with no certain savings plan to close it, is a material risk to refinancing capacity.
findings.figures: Budget deficit £26.7m in 2026/27; £60.3m in 2027/28
findings.quote: significant cumulative budget deficits were forecast of £26.7m in 2026/27, rising to £60.3m in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Quarter One 2025-26 reveals £29.6m forecast overspend despite 'balanced' budget approval
findings.detail: Even after building £52.3m of growth into the 2025-26 budget to address service pressures, budget monitoring at Q1 identified cost and demand pressures exceeding planning assumptions by £29.6m. The auditor explicitly states this threatens the planned reserve rebuild and could force 'difficult choices in 2026/27'.
findings.matters: A lender is concerned about budget execution risk and the council's ability to control spending. A £29.6m miss in just three months signals structural problems, not one-off issues.
findings.figures: £29.6m forecast overspend at Month Five 2025-26; £52.3m growth built into budget approval
findings.quote: budget monitoring at Quarter One 2025/26 identifies that cost and demand pressures are exceeding planning assumptions, with forecast budget pressures of £29.6m identified.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: General Fund balance depleted to £16.8m from £36.8m after £20.0m overspend in 2024-25
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget but experienced a net £20.0m revenue overspend, mainly in social care and homelessness. This forced a 54% drawdown of reserves from the recommended prudent level. The council now holds 'very low levels of reserves which impacts on its ability to respond to unforeseen financial pressures'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has financial headroom to absorb service shocks; at £16.8m reserves on a £1bn+ budget, it has essentially none.
findings.figures: General Fund balance reduced from £36.8m to £16.8m; net revenue overspend £20.0m
findings.quote: The net overspend was funded from the General Fund balance, reducing it from its recommended level of £36.8m to £16.8m at March 2025.

Returns in the first 8 months of the year averaged 4.25%, but the latest average return has dropped to 4.05% as the lower rate environment affects cash deposits and money market holdings.

findings.detail: The council arranged substantial new borrowing in Q3 comprising £70m from other local authorities at rates of 4.45%-4.50%, £5m from banks at 4.15%, and £40m from PWLB at rates of 4.62%-4.63%. This reflects ongoing capital financing to support the anticipated rise in capital financing requirements for the year.
findings.matters: The scale and cost of capital borrowing is a key indicator for lenders assessing the council's capital program funding strategy and debt servicing capacity

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee 061125 - Treasury Mid Year Report Final
findings.headline: Capital programme reprofiled with in-year borrowing need cut from £83m to £48m; reason not stated
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Strategy projected an £83m in-year borrowing requirement to finance the capital programme. The capital programme has since been reprofiled, reducing the projected borrowing need to £48m — a 42% reduction. The report provides no explanation for this material change, leaving unclear whether it reflects project deferrals or financial constraints.
findings.matters: A large reduction in planned capital financing needs explanation: it may signal either routine resequencing or reduced spending ambition driven by balance sheet pressure. The absence of explanation creates uncertainty about capital delivery plans.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee 061125 - Treasury Mid Year Report Final
findings.headline: Internal borrowing capacity is under pressure from forecast General Fund overspends and DSG deficits
findings.detail: The council has historically managed capital investment by using internal reserves and positive cashflows rather than external borrowing. However, the report explicitly states that forecast overspends in the General Fund and Dedicated Schools Grant are now constraining this approach. If these overspends remain unmitigated, balance sheet resources will be depleted, forcing the council to increase external borrowing beyond planned levels.
findings.matters: When reserves are consumed by operational shortfalls, a council's financial flexibility erodes and debt service costs rise. A lender needs to know whether the balance sheet can support both operating deficits and capital investment without destabilizing debt levels.
findings.figures: Actual borrowing at mid-year £949m; total long-term obligations £1,008.9m at 30/9/25; operational boundary for borrowing 2025/26 set at £1,098m
findings.quote: the council's ability to sustain previous levels of internal borrowing is increasingly under pressure due to forecast General Fund overspends and DSG deficits. If projected overspends remain unmitigated it will deplete the balance sheet resources used to support internal borrowing and has the potential to push up borrowing levels.

findings.paper_title: Income and Debt Recovery Assurance Audit Committee Nov 2025 (002)

findings.detail: The council wrote off £6.891m in council tax, £4.183m in sundry debt, £2.056m in Adult Social Care, and £0.569m in housing benefit overpayments. Write-offs are approved only after recovery options are exhausted, covering statute-barred debts, deceased residents with no estate, and residents who cannot be traced.
findings.matters: Write-offs reduce net recoverable revenue and show the council reaches practical limits in collecting various debts, affecting true cash-generative capacity.

findings.detail: The top 30 Adult Social Care debts total £3.86m. The council identifies Court of Protection applications and probate proceedings as the primary barrier to further recovery. These are judicial delays outside the council's control that prevent cash collection despite active recovery efforts.
findings.matters: These debts cannot be recovered on schedule due to procedural constraints in the court system, directly reducing the council's actual cash flow from recoverable receivables.

findings.quote: A key barrier to resolution pertains to ongoing delays in court processes, particularly in progressing Court of Protection applications and probate matters. These legal and procedural delays continue to impact recovery timelines, despite sustained efforts to move cases forward.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Children's Services remained inadequate at May 2023 Ofsted inspection; improvement continuing but not yet validated
findings.detail: Ofsted judged Children's Services inadequate overall in May 2023, with inadequate ratings in three key areas. The council has invested in improvement including new leadership and a transformation programme. Recent Ofsted monitoring visits (most recent March 2025) show progress in some areas (disabled children, missing children) but note gaps remain, particularly in multi-agency response to child exploitation and governance fragmentation.
findings.matters: Inadequate children's services is a reputational risk and can lead to higher intervention or council takeover. More immediately, improvement programmes are costly, and if they do not land before the next full inspection, the council faces further deterioration and potential for statutory direction.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Risk management not fully embedded across the council
findings.detail: The statement notes: 'Evidence suggests that risk management is not fully embedded across the Council and further work needs to be done to ensure a robust risk management culture and process exists and is operating effectively.' A risk management software solution is still in final testing. This is an area flagged for improvement in the 2025/26 work plan.
findings.matters: Weak risk management means the council may not identify emerging financial or operational problems early enough to manage them. Combined with low reserves and audit control weaknesses, this increases the risk of financial deterioration going unnoticed.

findings.quote: Evidence suggests that risk management is not fully embedded across the Council and further work needs to be done to ensure a robust risk management culture and process exists and is operating effectively.

findings.detail: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB is in financial turnaround and required to make 50% cuts to administrative costs. The ICB's budget constraints are focused on services not directly provided by NHS, including Continuing Health Care, Section 117 aftercare, SEND, and Better Care Fund services. The council states: 'The key risk is that the NHS will seek to reduce its expenditure in the expectation that the Council will meet costs of services to vulnerable adults and children to prevent harm.'
findings.matters: This is an external cost pressure. If the NHS withdraws funding for services the council is legally required to provide, the council's already-strained Adult Social Care and Children's Services budgets will face additional unfunded growth.

findings.quote: The key risk is that the NHS will seek to reduce its expenditure in the expectation that the Council will meet costs of services to vulnerable adults and children to prevent harm.

findings.detail: Adult Social Care and Health, Children and Young People's Services, and Neighbourhoods and Housing all overspent in 2024/25. From July 2024, budgetary controls were implemented to try to contain overspends at directorate level, but the outturn report in July 2025 shows these services still overran. findings.matters: Demand-led services (social care, housing) are difficult to control because the demand is determined by the size and characteristics of the population, not by the council's budget. Persistent overspends suggest the budget envelope is set below what the council must spend to meet legal duties.

findings.detail: The Director of Internal Audit's 2024/25 opinion is Limited Assurance rather than Reasonable Assurance. The opinion explicitly flags a high risk to the control environment. This reflects that governance, risk and control frameworks are mainly operating as intended but significant gaps remain.

news_drafts.headline: Liverpool forecasts £26.4m overspend on special needs funding, taking schools deficit to £38.6m
news_drafts.lead:
Liverpool City Council expects to overspend by £26.417m this year on high needs, the part of schools funding that pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The forecast, in the second-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) to Cabinet on 13 October, takes the total deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to £38.634m once £12.217m carried forward from 2025/26 is added.

The report says government has signalled a possible High Needs Stability Grant of about £6.917m, equal to 90% of the cumulative deficit to March 2026. Even with that grant, the paper says at least £5.300m would still have to be recovered from the council's General Fund, its main day-to-day budget, with the pressure extending into future years.

The report links the deficit to continuing rises in Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents that set out a child's support, and to more demand for places in non-maintained and independent special schools. Specialist provision is also still expanding, which affects capital spending (money spent on things that last) as well as day-to-day costs. SEN transport, which received £13.596m of budget growth, is currently forecast to come in on budget. The paper nonetheless calls it "a key financial risk for the council" and says performance will be monitored closely through the year.

news_drafts.headline: Liverpool council's reserves hit 'very low level' as financial pressures mount
news_drafts.lead:
Liverpool's reserves — money a council sets aside as a financial cushion — have fallen to £25.4m after overspends of £23.8m in 2024/25 and £11.7m in 2025/26. The council's chief finance officer said the council is now holding "a very low level of usable reserves which will reduce the ability of the council to manage its continuing financial challenges going forward."

The overspends were driven by demand-led service pressures: adult social care (£15.3m), children's services (£17.5m), and homelessness and transport (£21.2m). The council forecasts a cumulative budget gap—the difference between expected spending and available funding—of £63.9m by 2028/29. The council has raised council tax by the maximum allowed 4.99% for 2026/27, despite a 5.8% increase in government grant, signalling limited room for further local revenue-raising.
